c.tagline: Pakistan's cultural heart, where Mughal grandeur meets nonstop food streets.

taxi.fareNote: Metered street taxis are rare; agree a price before boarding. Most visitors use ride-hailing apps (Careem, inDrive, Uber), auto-rickshaws (negotiate the fare), or Bykea motorbike rides instead.

emergency.note: Rescue 1122 is the nationwide emergency ambulance and rescue service; dial 15 for police. Punjab Police also runs an 8787 helpline.

avoid.reason: Calmer than Karachi; caution at religious gatherings/rallies; petty crime

hood_desc: The historic core inside and around the old city walls, home to Lahore Fort, Badshahi Mosque, Wazir Khan Mosque, and the Fort Road Food Street; dense, atmospheric, and best for first-timers who want to be steps from the Mughal-era landmarks.

Lahore's modern commercial and lifestyle hub, centered on MM Alam Road and Main Boulevard with the city's top restaurants, cafes, malls, and hotels; suits travelers who want upscale dining and a convenient, well-connected base.

Defence Housing Authority, an expansive upscale planned suburb of wide leafy avenues, gated blocks, Packages Mall, and quiet residential streets; good for those wanting calm, security, and modern amenities away from the congestion.

A spacious, tree-lined garden suburb built around Model Town Park, with old-money bungalows, local markets, and a relaxed residential pace; suits families and travelers seeking a quieter, authentically local neighborhood.

The bustling bazaar district just south of the old city, famous for Anarkali Bazaar (one of South Asia's oldest markets), Food Street, and the Lahore Museum; ideal for shoppers and budget travelers wanting street life and history.

water.note: Groundwater and piped supplies are often polluted; use bottled or filtered water.

transit.hours: The Orange Line runs roughly 06:30-22:00 and the Metrobus about 06:00-22:00 daily; late-night travel relies on ride-hailing apps and rickshaws.
transit.note: Lahore has an elevated automated Orange Line Metro Train and the Metrobus (Green Line) BRT corridor, supplemented by Speedo feeder buses; ride-hailing apps and auto-rickshaws fill the gaps.
transit.pay: Flat fare of about Rs 40 per ride, paid with a stored-value transit card or single-journey token at station gates (cash to top up); the same card works across the Metrobus and Orange Line.

bus: Speedo feeder buses and local city buses
Daewoo Express and intercity coaches to other Pakistani cities
train: Pakistan Railways from Lahore Junction to Karachi, Rawalpindi/Islamabad, Multan, and Faisalabad

transit.m: Speedo feeder/local bus toward the city (limited; no direct metro link to the terminal)
Airport taxi to city center (30-40 min)

tip.r: ~10% at restaurants (a service charge is sometimes already added); small tips to porters, valets, and petrol-pump attendants are customary.

food.name: Nihari
food.desc: Beef shank stewed overnight in a marrow-rich, chilli-dark gravy, finished with ginger, green chilli and lemon and mopped up with khameeri roti.

places.name: Waris Nihari
places.note: Roadside institution with street seating; nihari with hot khasta naan straight from the tandoor.

places.name: Muhammadi Nihari House
places.note: Named by many locals as the city's best nihari, in beef and chicken versions.

places.name: Gawalmandi Food Street
places.note: Lahore's oldest food street; several nihari counters open from dawn.

food.name: Siri paye
food.desc: Head and trotters simmered all night into a gelatinous, spice-thick breakfast stew - the most Lahori meal there is.

places.name: Phajja Siri Paye
places.note: Running since 1947 and still the benchmark; go early, it sells out by mid-morning.

places.name: Gawalmandi Food Street
places.note: Rows of paye counters serving from around 6am alongside halwa puri stalls.

places.name: Muhammadi Nihari House
places.note: Paya as well as nihari, useful if you want both in one sitting.

food.name: Lahori chargha
food.desc: Whole chicken marinated in yoghurt and spice, steamed then deep-fried until the skin shatters; served with naan and chutney.

places.name: Tabaq Chargha
places.note: Repeatedly named the best chargha in town; the chowk is a chargha strip in itself.

places.name: Gawalmandi Food Street
places.note: The traditional place to head for chargha, eaten at pavement tables.

places.name: Anarkali Food Street
places.note: Cheap, busy and open late, with chargha alongside chaat and golgappay.

food.name: Butt karahi
food.desc: Chicken or mutton seared in a wok with tomato, green chilli, ginger and coriander until the fat separates - no cream, no shortcuts.

places.name: Butt Karahi Tikka Shop
places.note: The name locals give the dish; open late, plastic chairs on the street.

places.name: Haveli Restaurant
places.note: Karahi on a rooftop looking straight at the Badshahi Mosque.

places.name: Gawalmandi Food Street
places.note: Multiple karahi houses cooking to order in full view of the street.

food.name: Lahori fried fish
food.desc: Winter-season river fish rubbed with ajwain and gram flour, deep-fried in a huge kadhai and dusted with chaat masala.

places.name: Bashir Dar-ul-Mahi
places.note: The city's best-known fish house, at its peak from November to February.

places.name: Gawalmandi Food Street
places.note: Fish fryers set up on the street through the cold months.

places.name: Anarkali Food Street
places.note: Cheaper counters selling fish by weight with lemon and onion.

food.name: Falooda
food.desc: Layered dessert of vermicelli, basil seeds, rose syrup, milk and kulfi ice cream - the standard way to end a Lahori meal.

places.name: Chaman Ice Cream
places.note: Famous for kulfa-falooda; a Lahore dessert landmark for decades.

places.name: Gawalmandi Food Street
places.note: Falooda and kulfi carts stay open long after the kitchens close.

places.name: Nirala Sweets
places.note: Reliable sit-down chain for falooda, rabri and mithai.

food.name: Lassi
food.desc: Yoghurt churned with ice and either salt or sugar, served in a heavy steel tumbler; the standard chaser to a paye breakfast.

places.name: Bhati Gate lassi stalls
places.note: Clustered around Phajja; churned to order in wooden madhanis.

places.name: Gawalmandi Food Street
places.note: Sweet and salted lassi sold from breakfast until late morning.

places.name: Nirala Sweets
places.note: Air-conditioned option if you want lassi without the street heat.

food.name: Kashmiri chai
food.desc: Pink, faintly salty tea whipped with milk and topped with crushed pistachio and almond; a winter and wedding-season staple.

places.name: Gawalmandi Food Street
places.note: Chai counters serve pink tea with sheermal through the cold months.

places.name: Anarkali Food Street
places.note: Cheap cups poured all evening among the chaat stalls.

places.name: Liberty Market
places.note: Modern cafes and street carts both do a good pink chai here.

landmarks: Badshahi Mosque
One of the world's largest mosques, this red-sandstone Mughal masterpiece from 1673 dazzles with its vast courtyard, marble domes and intricate frescoes.
Lahore Fort (Shahi Qila)
This UNESCO-listed Mughal citadel houses the dazzling Sheesh Mahal mirror palace and centuries of imperial history behind its imposing red walls.
Shalimar Gardens
These UNESCO-listed 17th-century Mughal terraced gardens feature cascading fountains and reflecting pools, epitomizing the era's love of paradise-inspired landscape design.
Minar-e-Pakistan
This soaring minaret marks the spot where the 1940 Lahore Resolution was passed, standing as the towering national symbol of Pakistan's founding.
Wazir Khan Mosque
Renowned for its exquisite Kashi-kari tile mosaics and frescoes, this 17th-century mosque is considered one of the most ornately decorated in South Asia.
Wagah Border Ceremony
Witness the theatrical daily flag-lowering ritual between Pakistani and Indian soldiers, a high-energy spectacle of synchronized marching and patriotic fervor.
Tomb of Jahangir
The elaborately inlaid marble mausoleum of Mughal emperor Jahangir sits amid tranquil gardens in Shahdara, showcasing exceptional Mughal funerary architecture.
Data Darbar
South Asia's oldest Sufi shrine draws thousands of pilgrims daily to the resting place of the revered 11th-century saint Ali Hujwiri.
Anarkali Bazaar
One of South Asia's oldest surviving markets, this labyrinthine bazaar named after a legendary courtesan brims with textiles, jewelry, street food and centuries of lore.
Hazuri Bagh and Baradari
This elegant marble pavilion sits in a quadrangle bridging Lahore Fort and Badshahi Mosque, a peaceful garden square steeped in Sikh and Mughal history.

train.note: The Samjhauta Express to Delhi has been suspended since August 2019 and shows no sign of returning, so there is no working international train. Lahore Junction is a grand colonial station and the hub of the Punjab network, with the Green Line and Karakoram Express to Karachi taking 17-18 hours and frequent services to Rawalpindi in 4-5. Book on the Pakistan Railways site or app, or at the station; AC Business and Sleeper are the classes to aim for.

bus.note: The Delhi-Lahore bus has also been suspended, so there is no scheduled international coach. Travellers still cross to India on foot at Wagah, 25 km east, but only with an Indian visa arranged in advance and the crossing is often closed - check first. Daewoo Express (https://www.daewoo.com.pk/) and Faisal Movers run comfortable coaches from the Thokar Niaz Baig terminal to Islamabad in about 4-5 hours on the motorway, and to Multan and Karachi.

ferry.note: Lahore is inland in the Punjab on the Ravi river, which is not navigable, so there are no ferries. Pakistan's only passenger port is Karachi, about 1,200 km south, and it has no scheduled passenger service either.

half.name: Hiran Minar
half.blurb: A Mughal-era hunting lodge and tower about an hour from Lahore, built by Emperor Jahangir beside a large artificial lake.

half.name: Changa Manga Forest
half.blurb: A large man-made forest plantation outside Lahore with a boating lake, a narrow-gauge scenic train, and dense stands of planted trees.

full.name: Katas Raj Temples
full.blurb: A Hindu temple complex in the Chakwal district about 2.5 hours from Lahore, built around a sacred pond linked to Shiva mythology.

full.name: Rohtas Fort
full.blurb: A 16th-century Sher Shah Suri garrison fort near Jhelum, a UNESCO World Heritage Site about two hours from Lahore with massive stone walls.
